summary: Specifies how to find authoritative RADIUS servers for a given realm using DNS, for use with RADIUS over TLS or DTLS. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7585 lets a RADIUS server find out who handles a user's realm by asking DNS, the same way a mail server finds where to deliver mail. It also defines a new field in a server's certificate that says which realms that server is allowed to look after, so the answer can be checked.

how does radius find a server for a realm
what is the nairealm certificate field
subtitle: Finding the RADIUS server that owns a user's realm by asking DNS, then proving the server is allowed to answer.

tldr.problem: Every RADIUS transport needs its peers configured by hand, so a roaming network with many realms ends up with a long list of forwarding servers to maintain, and every change has to be pushed to every branch.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a lookup that turns the realm part of a user name into DNS NAPTR and SRV records naming the authoritative server, and a new X.509 certificate property that lets the server state which realms it is authorized to serve.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document. The memo says it expects the choice points it leaves open to be trimmed down once a Standards Track version is written.

today: RFC 7585 is an Experimental document from October 2015, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo says the duration of the experiment is undetermined, and that once enough experience is collected on the choice points it leaves open, it is expected to be obsoleted by a Standards Track version that trims those choice points down.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RADIUS in all its current transport variants, RADIUS over UDP, TCP, TLS and DTLS, requires manual configuration of all peers, both clients and servers.

Where more than one administrative entity collaborates for RADIUS authentication of their respective customers, a roaming consortium, the Network Access Identifier is the suggested way of differentiating users between those entities. The part of a username to the right of the at sign in such an identifier is called the user's realm. Where many realms and RADIUS forwarding servers are in use, the number of realms to be forwarded and the corresponding number of servers to configure may be significant. Where new realms with new servers are added, or details of existing servers change on a regular basis, maintaining a single monolithic configuration file for all of these details may prove too cumbersome to be useful.

There is extra complexity when a consortium consists of independently working branches, such as departments and national subsidiaries, each with its own forwarding servers and each adding or changing its realm lists at its own discretion, because the changed data has to be synchronized across all branches.

Where realms can be partitioned, for example according to their top-level domain ending, forwarding of requests can be realized with a hierarchy of RADIUS servers, each serving its partition of the realm space. But such partitioning is not always possible. In one real-life deployment the administrative boundaries and RADIUS forwarding servers are organized along country borders, but generic top-level domains such as .edu do not map to that choice of boundaries. These situations benefit significantly from a distributed mechanism for storing realm and server reachability information. This document describes one such mechanism: storage of realm-to-server mappings in DNS, so that realm-based request forwarding can be realized without a static hierarchy.

The memo also specifies various approaches for verifying that server information retrieved from DNS came from an authorized party. The reason is that an organization which is not at all part of a given roaming consortium may alter its own DNS records to yield a result for its own realm. The memo describes the approach as very similar to the one taken with the Diameter protocol, so the basic idea of using NAPTR records in DNS domains that match NAI realms is not of a very experimental nature, but the memo offers a few choice points and extensions beyond the Diameter provisions: provisions for determining the authority of a server to act for users of a realm, which were declared out of scope for Diameter; much more in-depth guidance on DNS regarding timeouts, failure conditions and alteration of time-to-live information; and a partially correct routing error detection during DNS lookups.
sections.plainLanguage: Today every RADIUS server has to be told in advance which other servers exist, and in a roaming network with many realms that list grows and changes constantly. This memo replaces the list with a DNS lookup, and then adds a check so that the answer cannot simply be faked by whoever owns the domain.

sections.title: The DNS Records and the Certificate Property
sections.content:
DNS definitions of RADIUS/TLS servers can be either S-NAPTR records or SRV records, and when both are defined the resolution algorithm prefers the S-NAPTR results.

The memo defines three S-NAPTR service tags: aaa+auth for RADIUS Authentication, aaa+acct for RADIUS Accounting and aaa+dynauth for RADIUS Dynamic Authorization. It defines two S-NAPTR protocol tags: radius.tls.tcp for RADIUS transported over TLS and radius.dtls.udp for RADIUS transported over DTLS. The delimiter in the protocol tags is only a separator for human reading convenience, not for structure or namespacing, and it must not be parsed in any way by the querying application or resolver. It defines two SRV prefixes as well, _radiustls._tcp and _radiusdtls._udp.

Because the discovery algorithm has no provisions to establish confidential keying material between the client and the server it discovers, pre-shared key ciphersuites for TLS cannot be used in the subsequent handshake, and only ciphersuites using X.509 certificates can be used. The memo defines one mandatory-to-implement mechanism for verifying that the contacted host is authoritative for a realm, and gives an example of another mechanism in widespread deployment and one possible approach based on DNSSEC, which it describes as yet unimplemented.

The mandatory mechanism is trust roots plus the NAIRealm certificate property. Verification is a two-step process. The first step is the verification of certificate well-formedness and validity, and whether it was issued from a root certificate the client deems trustworthy. The second step compares the realm derived from the user name, after any consortium name mangling, against all values of the contacted server's X.509 certificate property subjectAlternativeName:otherName:NAIRealm.

The NAIRealm property is a new subjectAltName field, because the existing subjectAltName:dNSName is syntactically a good match but would inappropriately conflate DNS names and NAI realm names. It holds either a single NAI realm name or a wildcard name matching a set of realms. It may substitute the leftmost dot-separated label of an NAI with a single asterisk to mean all labels in that part; other wildcard forms, such as a number of characters followed by an asterisk to indicate a common prefix, are not permitted. The comparison with the realm derived from user input is byte by byte, except that an optional leftmost part whose content is a single asterisk matches all strings in the same dot-separated part. If at least one of the NAIRealm values matches, the server is considered authorized; if none match, it is unauthorized. The memo gives a table of matching examples, including cases where a realm such as bar.foo.example does not match the certificate value *.example, because the wildcard only covers the leftmost part.

The second mechanism compares the certificate's Policy OID extensions with a configured list of acceptable OIDs for the consortium. The memo says this is inferior, because all authorized servers are validated by the same OID value, so it cannot express authority for one specific realm within the consortium. The third mechanism uses DNSSEC and DANE: the DANE TLSA records of all authorized servers are put into a DNSSEC zone rooted in a common consortium-agreed branch of the DNS tree, the entity executing the algorithm retrieves the TLSA records for the label formed from the realm and the common branch, and verifies that the certificate presented during the handshake matches the TLSA record. The memo notes that even then the server still has to present a certificate proving its authority to serve a particular realm.
sections.plainLanguage: Three tags in DNS say which service is being looked up: authentication, accounting or dynamic authorization, over either TLS or DTLS. The certificate check compares the realm in the user name against a new field in the server's certificate, which may allow a wildcard on the first part of the realm.

sections.title: The Resolution Algorithm
sections.content:
The input to the algorithm for authentication and accounting discovery is the RADIUS User-Name attribute with content of the form user at realm. The use of multiple at signs is strongly discouraged, but if present the last one is the separator and the earlier ones are part of the local user identifier. For dynamic authorization discovery the input is the domain name of the operator of a realm as communicated during user authentication with the Operator-Name attribute, preceded with an at sign. The memo notes that the User-Name attribute is defined to contain UTF-8 text, but the content may or may not be UTF-8, and implementors must take possible conversion error paths into consideration. The document describes server discovery only for well-formed realms that map to DNS domain names in UTF-8, and the result of all other contents is unspecified.

The output is a two-tuple: a set of tuples holding hostname, port, protocol, order or preference, and an effective time-to-live, which may be empty, together with an integer. If the set is empty the integer holds the effective time-to-live to use as a backoff timeout; if the set is not empty the integer is zero and unused.

The algorithm has twenty steps. It finds the position of the last at sign in the input and takes the substring after it as the realm. It modifies the realm according to agreed consortium procedures if applicable, and converts it to a representation usable by the name resolution library if needed. It starts a timer, and if the timer reaches the DNS timeout it continues at step twenty, which produces an empty set and a backoff time and logs an error.

It then performs a NAPTR query for the realm. If the result is a negative DNS response, the effective time-to-live of the SOA record is taken and the algorithm continues at step thirteen; if name resolution returns with an error, the result is an empty set with a backoff time, and the algorithm terminates. It extracts the NAPTR records with the service tags for authentication, accounting or dynamic authorization as appropriate, keeping note of the protocol tag and the remaining time-to-live of each. If no records are found it continues at step thirteen.

For the extracted records it performs successive resolution as defined for S-NAPTR. An implementation may use greedy result evaluation, running the rest of the algorithm for the highest-order entry and only looking up the remainder if necessary. If the set of host names is empty, the result is an empty set with a backoff time. Otherwise the set of host names, ports, protocols, preferences and effective time-to-live values is formed and the algorithm continues at step eighteen.

Step thirteen generates a name by prefixing the realm with the SRV labels, and step fourteen performs the SRV lookup. A name resolution error gives an empty set and a backoff time, and a negative DNS response gives an empty set with the smaller of the two backoff values. Step eighteen resolves the host names into A and AAAA addresses to form the final set. Step nineteen then tests each element of the result against the address and port on which the original request was received. If the result contains the server's own listening address there is a potential for an endless forwarding loop, so the algorithm aborts, returns an empty set with a backoff time, and logs an error.
sections.plainLanguage: The lookup strips the user name off the at sign, asks DNS for a NAPTR record for what is left, follows that to an SRV record, and resolves that to an address and port. The last step checks that the answer is not the server's own address, which would mean it would be talking to itself forever.

sections.title: When Discovery Runs and How Long to Wait
sections.content:
Dynamic server discovery as defined in the memo is only applicable for new AAA transactions and per service, so distinct discovery is needed for Authentication, Accounting and Dynamic Authorization, and only where a RADIUS entity acting as a forwarding server receives a request with a realm for which it is not authoritative and for which no explicit next hop is configured. It applies to new user sessions, meaning the initial Access-Request, since subsequent messages such as Access-Challenges and Access-Accepts use the previously established channel between client and server; to the first accounting ticket for a user session; and to the first dynamic authorization packet for a user session.

The algorithm has three configurable timing variables with default values. The DNS timeout is the maximum amount of time to wait for the complete set of all DNS queries to complete, defaulting to 3 seconds. The minimum effective time-to-live is the minimum DNS time-to-live of discovered targets, defaulting to 60 seconds. The backoff time is how long to wait before attempting dynamic discovery again if no conclusive DNS response was retrieved after the timeout, defaulting to 600 seconds. The effective time-to-live of a set of results is the largest of the minimum effective time-to-live and the smallest of the DNS time-to-live values that led to the result.

The memo explains why the algorithm controls its own execution time with a timer rather than waiting for the name resolution library: the lookup destination is derived from uncontrollable user input, so if those outside entities are misconfigured or unreachable the algorithm might take an unacceptably long time to terminate, and many RADIUS implementations time out after five seconds between request and response. Execution should be non-blocking, so that other requests can be processed while the algorithm runs.

On validity, the memo notes that the discovery algorithm is used by servers that do not have sufficient configuration information to process an incoming request on their own, so if the result contains the server's own listening address there is a potential for an endless forwarding loop. If the listening address is the DNS result with the highest priority the server enters a tight loop; if it has a lower priority there is a potential loop with intermediate hops in between. The underlying reason is that the server is seriously misconfigured in not recognizing the request as one to be processed by itself, and RADIUS has no built-in loop detection. The memo says the safeguard does not provide perfect protection, since a subsequent hop may have a statically configured next hop leading back into the loop, or greedy result evaluation may have skipped the branch containing the server's own address.

While a connection to a home server can remain open for an indefinite time, the time-to-live values in the name resolution system indicate how long it is safe to rely on the results, and very low values would cause thrashing of connections. When a connection is open and the effective time-to-live learned during discovery has not expired, subsequent new user sessions for that realm should reuse the existing connection and should neither re-execute the algorithm nor open a new connection, and the server should re-execute the algorithm once the effective time-to-live has expired while keeping the session open during that reassessment. If the algorithm ends with an empty set, the server should not attempt another execution for the same target realm before the timeout has passed.
sections.plainLanguage: Discovery runs once per new session, not on every packet, and only when the server has no configured answer. It gives up after three seconds and then stays quiet for ten minutes, so a broken DNS cannot be used to hammer the server. While a connection is open and its answer is still fresh, new sessions reuse it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
When DNS is used without DNSSEC security extensions and validation for all of the replies to NAPTR, SRV and A or AAAA requests, the result of the discovery process cannot be trusted. Even if it can be trusted, actual authorization of the discovered server to provide service for the given realm needs to be verified, and a mechanism from the certificate verification section or equivalent must be used.

The lookup of DNS resource records based on unverified user input is an attack vector for denial-of-service attacks: an attacker might intentionally craft bogus DNS zones that take a very long time to reply, for example because of a particularly byzantine tree structure or artificial delays in responses. To mitigate this, implementations should consider rate limiting either the number of new executions of the discovery algorithm as a whole, or the number of intermediate responses to track, or at least the number of pending DNS queries. Implementations may choose lower values than the default for the DNS timeout to limit the impact of such attacks, and may also continue trying to resolve DNS records after the timeout has passed, since a subsequent request for the same realm might benefit from the results anyway.

With dynamic discovery enabled, and depending on the deployment scenario, the server may need to open its target address and port to the entire Internet, because arbitrary clients may discover it as a target for their authentication requests. If such clients are not part of the roaming consortium, the RADIUS/TLS connection setup phase will fail, which is intended, but the computational cost of the connection attempt is significant. When the port for a TLS-based service is open, the RADIUS server shares all the typical attack vectors for services based on TLS, and deployments should consider these and take appropriate countermeasures, such as blacklisting known bad addresses on a firewall or rate limiting new connection attempts.
sections.plainLanguage: A lookup driven by whatever a user typed is a way to make the server do expensive work on demand, so the number of lookups has to be limited. And once a server can be found by anyone, its TLS port is exposed to the usual attacks on TLS services, so the usual countermeasures apply.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The classic RADIUS operational model, with known preconfigured peers, shared secret security and mostly plaintext communication, differs significantly from the new dynamic discovery model, with peer discovery through DNS, public key infrastructure security and packet confidentiality, in their impact on the privacy of end users trying to authenticate.

With classic RADIUS, traffic in large environments gets aggregated by statically configured clearinghouses, and the packets sent to those clearinghouses and their responses are mostly unprotected. All intermediate IP hops can therefore inspect most of the packet payload in clear text, including the User-Name and Calling-Station-Id attributes, and can observe which client sent the packet to which clearinghouse, which allows the creation of mobility profiles for any passive observer on the IP path. The existence of a central clearinghouse also creates an opportunity for the clearinghouse to create the same mobility profiles, whether or not it is trusted not to. And because the clearinghouse is a RADIUS intermediate in possession of a valid shared secret, it can observe and record even security-critical attributes such as User-Password, a risk that may be mitigated by choosing authentication payloads that are cryptographically secured and do not use the User-Password attribute, such as certain EAP types. There is no additional information disclosure to parties outside the IP path, in particular no DNS servers learn about realms of current ongoing authentications.

With RADIUS and dynamic discovery, the protocol allows RADIUS clients to identify and directly connect to the RADIUS home server. This can eliminate the use of clearinghouses to forward requests, and it eliminates the ability of the clearinghouse to aggregate the user information flowing through it, although there are reasons why clearinghouses might still be used, such as acting as a gateway for multiple backends in a company, or a requirement to sanitize RADIUS datagrams. Even where intermediate proxies continue to be used for unrelated reasons, the number of such proxies may be reduced by removing those deployed purely for routing, which reduces the number of entities able to inspect the traffic.

On the other side, RADIUS clients using dynamic discovery query the Domain Name System and use a user's realm name as the query label. A passive observer on the path between the RADIUS client and the DNS servers can learn that a user of that realm was trying to authenticate at that client at a certain time, which may or may not be enough to create a mobility profile. During the recursive DNS resolution, a fair number of DNS servers and the hops in between get to learn that information, and because not every authentication triggers a DNS lookup there is no one-to-one relation between leaked realm information and the number of authentications for that realm. Since dynamic discovery operates hop by hop, there is also no guarantee that the RADIUS payload is not transmitted between RADIUS systems that do not use this algorithm and may use other transports such as RADIUS over UDP, and on such hops the enhanced privacy is jeopardized.

The memo summarizes the trade-off: with classic RADIUS, few intermediate entities learn very detailed data about every ongoing authentication, while with dynamic discovery, many entities learn only very little about recently authenticated realms.
sections.plainLanguage: The old model concentrated user information in a few servers that could see it all. The new model spreads the information out, so many servers see only a little, but a DNS lookup reveals which realm someone is logging in to, and the DNS servers involved learn that too.

viz.caption: THE DISCOVERY LOOKUP, STEP BY STEP

messages.label: NAPTR QUERY
messages.note: Asks which server is authoritative for the realm.

messages.label: SRV QUERY
messages.note: Asks for the host name, port and priority.

messages.label: SRV ANSWER
messages.note: Returns the host name and port, in preference order.

messages.label: RADIUS/TLS CONNECTION
messages.note: The server is contacted and its certificate checked for authority over the realm.

viz.caption: THE THREE WAYS TO CHECK THAT A SERVER IS AUTHORIZED

items.title: Trust roots plus NAIRealm
items.text: The mandatory mechanism. The server's certificate must carry a new subjectAltName field naming the realm, with a wildcard allowed on the leftmost part.

items.title: Trust roots plus policyOID
items.text: The certificate's Policy OID extensions are compared with a configured list. All authorized servers share one value, so it cannot express authority for one realm.

items.title: DNSSEC and DANE
items.text: Proves the DNS answer was authentic and ties the server certificate to the realm, but the server still has to prove it is a consortium member.
